intro.title: Introduction
intro.body_md: You are an associate at Ellingboe & Ravndal LLP, and your client is Travis Wenzloff, a forty-three-year-old commercial HVAC technician charged in the Minnesota District Court for Sherburne County with Third-Degree Driving While Impaired. Travis holds a Class A commercial driver's license and drives a service truck to job sites every day, so his livelihood rides entirely on that credential. On a subzero January night, after a fourteen-hour double shift and a stop for beers on the way home, he was pulled over on Highway 10 following a citizen's report of a weaving vehicle. A deputy ran field sobriety tests on an ice-packed shoulder in extreme cold, and an evidentiary breath test at the jail reported an alcohol concentration of 0.09 — just over the per-se line. Travis tells you he was exhausted and distracted, not drunk, and that a prescription cough syrup and a mouthwash he used before driving may have skewed the reading. A prior impaired-driving incident several years back has pushed the stakes higher and threatens his commercial license for good. This exercise puts you in the first client interview and the strategic work that follows. Your job is to gather the facts — including the ones Travis is ashamed to volunteer — spot the issues in the stop, the field tests, and the breath sample, counsel a frightened client whose career is on the line, and build a plan that treats the license as the real prize. Everything you need is in the case file; the law is yours to research.

objectives.title: Learning Objectives
objectives.body_md: By completing this exercise you will practice and be assessed on a defined set of lawyering skills and tasks. First, **fact gathering (SK-LP-07 / TSK-022, TSK-023, TSK-025)**: conduct a client interview that builds a reliable timeline of the shift, the drinking, the stop, the field tests, and the breath test, and that earns the sensitive facts — the fatigue-and-phone distraction behind the weaving, the mouthwash used to mask the smell of beer, an uncounted third drink, and a prior offense the client cannot bring himself to raise — which surface only when the client trusts you. Second, **diagnosis and issue-spotting (SK-LP-01 / TSK-001, TSK-004)**: identify the legal vulnerabilities in the reasonable-suspicion basis for the stop, in field sobriety tests run in extreme cold on ice, and in a 0.09 breath reading exposed to mouth-alcohol and margin-of-error challenges. Third, **procedural framework (SK-LP-04)**: track the two parallel proceedings — the criminal charge and the civil implied-consent license revocation — and their separate clocks. Fourth, **counseling a distressed client (SK-LP-10 / TSK-034, TSK-037)**: address Travis's fear for his CDL and his family's income, explain what happens next, and set expectations without over-promising. Fifth, **negotiation strategy (SK-LP-13 / TSK-044, TSK-045)**: prepare a plea-and-negotiation plan that protects the commercial license. Sixth, **professional responsibility (SK-LP-16 / TSK-060)**: observe the no-contact rule with the represented arresting deputy and stay within the scope of the flat-fee engagement. These objectives map directly to the assessment and feedback rubric for the matter.

activities.title: Activities
activities.body_md: This matter unfolds across several assessed and rehearsal activities that mirror the Practicum's DWI arc. (1) **Preliminary case analysis.** Read the full case file and produce a short case-analysis memorandum identifying the charge and its degree, the elements the State must prove, the parallel implied-consent proceeding, and the defense's best factual and legal openings. (2) **Client interview.** Conduct a recorded interview with Travis Wenzloff through the simulated-client engine. Open with rapport and confidentiality, funnel from open-ended narrative to targeted probing, and reach the practical fear — his commercial license — that is driving him. Several facts will not come out unless you earn them. (3) **Strategy and negotiation plan.** Draft a strategic settlement-and-negotiation plan (SSNP) that weighs suppression against a negotiated resolution and keeps the CDL consequence at the center. (4) **Plea negotiation.** Conduct a simulated negotiation with the prosecution toward a resolution that protects the commercial license. (5) **Contested omnibus and implied-consent preparation.** Outline the suppression arguments you would raise at the omnibus hearing and the issues you would press at the implied-consent review. Rehearsal runs are unlimited; the assessed events are the interview, the written work, and the negotiation.

instructions.title: Instructions
instructions.body_md: Work only from the materials in this packet and the case file; the substantive law is yours to find and apply through your own research. Submit three written work products on the posted schedule: (a) a four-page preliminary case-analysis memorandum; (b) a strategic settlement-and-negotiation plan; and (c) a one-page client-advice letter summarizing Travis's options and the immediate steps on both his regular and his commercial driving privileges. For the client interview, you must complete at least one recorded run through the simulated-client engine before the assessed interview; your rapport and questioning technique are scored on how much of the reliable record you elicit and how you handle a client who is frightened for his livelihood. For the negotiation, prepare a written position and target before the session. **Professional-responsibility instruction:** do not attempt to interview Deputy Kallestad directly — he is a witness for the State and is represented through the county attorney's office; any request for his account goes through the prosecutor. Cite no legal authority in client-facing documents; save citations for internal analysis. Observe every deadline; the implied-consent review in particular runs on a short statutory clock, and late written work is penalized under the course rules. All oral events require professional attire.

history.title: Procedural and Factual History
history.body_md: The stop and arrest occurred on the night of Friday, January 17, 2025, on eastbound Highway 10 in Sherburne County during a subzero cold snap. Deputy Reid Kallestad of the Sherburne County Sheriff's Office responded to a citizen's 911 report of a dark pickup weaving, located a matching vehicle, followed it for roughly a mile and a half, observed it touch the fog line once, and stopped it at 10:58 p.m. He conducted standardized field sobriety tests on an ice-packed shoulder in extreme cold, administered a preliminary roadside breath test, and arrested Travis Wenzloff. At the Sherburne County Jail a certified operator administered an evidentiary breath test on a DataMaster DMT, which reported an alcohol concentration of 0.09. Travis was read the Implied Consent Advisory and served with a notice of license revocation. Because his driving record reflects a prior impaired-driving incident, the State charged the current offense as Third-Degree Driving While Impaired. Travis was released the following morning; his vehicle had been towed. He retained Ellingboe & Ravndal LLP on January 22, 2025. A not-guilty plea was entered, the defense served a demand for discovery, filed a timely petition for judicial review of the implied-consent revocation, and requested a contested omnibus hearing on probable cause and suppression. As of the simulation date, the omnibus hearing is pending, the implied-consent review is pending, and no plea has been reached. The commercial-license consequence remains the client's overriding concern.

considerations.title: Considerations
considerations.body_md: Several threads deserve early attention. The **stop** rests on a citizen's weaving report plus limited independent observation — a single touch of the fog line over a mile and a half of following. Consider how reliable the tip was, whether the reporting motorist could even confirm the stopped truck was the one she watched, and how much the deputy corroborated on his own; the dashcam is the record that tests all of this. The **field sobriety tests** were performed on an ice-packed shoulder at roughly four below zero, in wind, by a man who had just worked a fourteen-hour day and who lives with a reflux condition — each of which bears on how much weight balance-based testing can carry. The **breath sample** reads 0.09, only just over the per-se line, so the instrument's stated measurement uncertainty and a possible mouth-alcohol event — an alcohol-based cough syrup, an alcohol-containing mouthwash used minutes before driving, reflux during the observation period, and a question whether that period was truly continuous — are not academic; they may be the difference between a per-se case and no per-se case. Weigh **suppression against negotiation**, but never lose sight of the **two clocks**: the criminal charge and the civil implied-consent revocation move separately, and the revocation reaches the client's license first. Above all, keep the **commercial-license consequence** at the center: for a CDL holder a second qualifying incident is a career-ending, lifetime disqualification, and that — not jail — is what your client actually needs you to fight. Mind the no-contact rule as you gather the other side's account.

substantive_info.title: Substantive Information
substantive_info.body_md: This is an impaired-driving prosecution in Minnesota, elevated above a first-offense level by a prior incident within the look-back period, in which the State also pursues an administrative revocation of the client's license through the implied-consent process. You will need to research, in the assigned jurisdiction, the standards that govern each pressure point in this file: the level of suspicion required for a lawful traffic stop, and how a citizen tip together with an officer's own observations does or does not supply it; the evidentiary treatment and known limitations of standardized field sobriety tests, particularly when administered off level ground, in extreme cold, and on a fatigued subject; the foundational requirements and the margin-of-error and mouth-alcohol challenges applicable to evidentiary breath testing, including the significance of a pre-test observation period and of alcohol-containing oral products and reflux; and the implied-consent framework that governs both the admissibility of the breath sample and the administrative revocation, along with the separate and heightened consequences that attach to a commercial driver's license. You should also research the mechanics of charge reduction and plea negotiation where a prior offense drives the degree of the charge, and the professional-conduct rule governing communication with a person represented by counsel, which controls how you may approach the State's law-enforcement witness. The case file gives you the facts; the controlling law is the object of your research and is not supplied here.
